blocks.text: What public finance is

text.text: is the field of economics that analyses government taxation and spending policies. It looks at how the taxing and spending of government influence two things: the
(what the economy produces and with which inputs) and the
The same field is also called

blocks.text: Microeconomic functions = allocation and distribution. Macroeconomic questions (unemployment, inflation, stabilisation of the business cycle) are usually left to macroeconomics. Example: a tax on cigarettes changes how many cigarettes are produced (allocation) and who carries the cost (distribution).
blocks.title: Background (not in course slides)

blocks.text: The curriculum says the exam can ask where the Latin words come from. "Public" comes from Latin publicus, "of the people, belonging to the state". "Finance" goes back to Latin finis, "end", in the sense of settling (ending) a debt or payment. "Fiscal" comes from Latin fiscus, the basket in which the Roman state kept its money, which came to mean the state treasury. Check the wording your professor used in the lecture.
blocks.title: Where the words come from (curriculum topic; not in course slides)

blocks.text: Public finance and ideology: two views of government
How much government should do depends on how we see the relation between the individual and the state. The slides contrast two views.

rows: Society is a natural organism; government is its heart
Government is a contrivance (a tool) erected to further individual goals
Valued only by their contribution to realising social goals
The individual is what counts; government exists for individuals
Organic part of society; the community is stressed above the individual
Not an organic part of society; created by individuals for individuals

text.text: individuals are like the parts of a body. A part has meaning only as part of the whole, so a person matters only as a member of the community. The goals of society are decided by the government, and a person's worth is measured by how much they contribute to reaching those goals.
government is a device that people build because it helps them reach their own goals. It is not part of society by nature. Government is created by individuals, for individuals.

blocks.text: Rosen adds that people who share the mechanistic view still disagree about how much government should do: libertarians want a minimal state, while social democrats accept a large role in redistribution and regulation. The textbook itself takes the mechanistic view, which is why it judges policies by their effect on individual welfare.

blocks.text: Regulation can cost the economy a great deal without appearing as government spending. Example: a rule that every firm must install a filter costs firms money, but the cost never shows up in the unified budget. The regulatory budget tries to make this cost visible.

blocks.text: What a public good is

text.text: are introduced as the general welfare of the people, the best interests of the community. In economics, a good is classified by two properties of its consumption: whether it is

items.text: when one person consumes the good, less is left for others. If I eat a sandwich, you cannot eat the same sandwich.

one person's consumption does not reduce the amount available to others. My protection by national defence does not reduce yours. (Rosen: the marginal cost of serving one more consumer is zero; not in course slides.)
it is possible to stop people who do not pay from consuming it. A cinema can refuse entry without a ticket.
it is impossible, or extremely costly, to stop anyone from consuming it. A lighthouse's light is seen by every ship.

blocks.text: Three definitions from the slides

items.text: – a commodity that is nonrival and nonexcludable in consumption. Example: national defence.
– a commodity that is rival and excludable in consumption. Example: a pizza, a pair of shoes.
– a good that is rival and/or excludable to some extent. Example: a road that becomes congested at rush hour, or a public swimming pool with an entry fee.

blocks.text: Types of goods (the slide's matrix)

rows: NATURAL MONOPOLY (cable TV, an uncongested toll road)
COMMON RESOURCES (fish in the sea, a public pasture)

blocks.text: Start from the two extremes: private goods are YES/YES, public goods are NO/NO. The mixed cases: natural monopoly = you can be excluded but you do not use it up; common resources = you cannot be excluded but you do use it up. Examples in the table are illustrations, not from the slides.
blocks.title: How to remember the matrix

blocks.text: Common resources tend to be overused because nobody can be excluded and each user reduces what is left for others ("tragedy of the commons": overfishing). Natural monopoly goods are often provided by one firm because once the network exists, serving one more user costs almost nothing.
blocks.title: Background (not in course slides)

blocks.text: Efficient provision of public goods

text.text: For a private good the market demand curve is built by

: the process of creating a market demand curve by summing the quantities demanded by each individual at every price. At a price of €2, if Ana wants 3 units and Ivo wants 5, the market demand at €2 is 8 units. Each person buys a different quantity at the same price.
when supply and demand are EQUAL.
For a public good everyone consumes the same quantity (the same level of defence protects everyone), so we cannot add quantities. Instead we use

: the process of creating an aggregate demand curve for a public good by adding the prices each individual is willing to pay for a given quantity of the good. If, for one more fireworks show, Ana would pay €6 and Ivo €4, society values that unit at €10.

rows: Prices (willingness to pay), at each quantity

blocks.text: A public good is provided efficiently when the sum of everyone's willingness to pay for one more unit equals the marginal cost of producing it (Samuelson rule: ΣMRS = MRT). In the example, produce another show only if it costs no more than €10.
blocks.title: Efficiency rule (not in course slides)

blocks.text: The free-rider problem

text.text: – the incentive to let other people pay for a public good while you enjoy the benefits. Because a public good is nonexcludable, you get it whether you pay or not, so many people hide how much they value it. As a result, a private market tends to provide too little of a public good, or none at all. This is the main reason why government often provides public goods and finances them with taxes.

blocks.text: Example: residents of a street are asked to contribute to street lighting. Each one reasons that the lights will be built anyway if the neighbours pay, so each contributes less than the lights are worth to them.
Perfect price discrimination

text.text: is when a producer charges each person the maximum he or she is willing to pay for the good. In theory this would let a private firm collect exactly each person's valuation and so supply a public good efficiently. (Not in course slides: in practice the firm cannot know everyone's true willingness to pay, which is exactly what free riders hide.)

blocks.text: Privatization

text.text: is the process of turning services that are supplied by the government over to the private sector for provision and/or production.

blocks.text: Provision = deciding that the good is supplied and paying for it. Production = actually making it. Government can provide a good without producing it: it can pay a private firm to collect rubbish, so provision is public and production is private.
blocks.title: Provision vs. production (not in course slides)

blocks.text: The slides list four criteria for deciding between public and private production:

items.text: – who can produce more cheaply? Private firms may pay lower wages or buy materials more cheaply.
– contracting out has costs too: writing contracts, supervising the private producer, checking quality.
– when people want very different things (e.g. different kinds of schools), private supply can offer more variety than one uniform public service.
: some commodities ought to be made available to everybody (e.g. basic education, health care), whatever their income.

blocks.text: The slides treat public goods as a special kind of externality: when a public good is provided, everyone benefits, also those who did not pay. T3 develops this idea.

blocks.text: What an externality is

text.text: is a cost or benefit that occurs when the activity of one entity directly affects the welfare of another in a way that is outside the market mechanism. "Outside the market" means that nobody pays or gets paid for the effect: a factory that pollutes a river does not pay the fishermen downstream, and the fishermen cannot charge the factory.

items.text: – an external cost: pollution, noise, congestion, second-hand smoke.
– an external benefit: a beekeeper's bees pollinate a neighbour's orchard; a vaccinated person protects others.

blocks.text: A producer looks only at its own (private) cost. With a negative externality, the cost to society is higher than the private cost (marginal social cost = marginal private cost + marginal damage), so the market produces too much. With a positive externality, the market produces too little.
blocks.title: Why markets get it wrong (not in course slides)

blocks.text: Four characteristics of externalities (slides)

items.text: Externalities can be produced by consumers as well as firms.
A neighbour playing loud music at night or a smoker in a closed room creates an externality just like a polluting factory.

It is not simply that A harms B: the problem exists because A and B want to use the same resource in incompatible ways. The river can be a dump for the factory or a clean fishery, not both. Stopping the factory would in turn impose a cost on the factory.
Not every external effect is harmful: research, education and pollination create benefits for others.
Public goods can be viewed as a special kind of externality.
When someone provides a public good, everyone else benefits too, without paying: a positive externality that reaches the whole community (link to T2).

blocks.text: Private solution: the Coase theorem

text.text: – provided that transaction costs are negligible, an efficient solution to an externality problem is achieved as long as someone is assigned property rights, independent of who is assigned those rights.
once property rights are established, government intervention is not required to deal with externalities. The parties bargain with each other.

blocks.text: Example: if the fishermen own the river, the factory must pay them for the right to pollute; if the factory owns it, the fishermen can pay the factory to pollute less. In both cases they bargain until the pollution level is efficient. Who gets the right changes who pays whom (the distribution of income), but not the efficient outcome.

The theorem needs low transaction costs. It breaks down when very many parties are involved (millions of people breathing polluted air cannot bargain with every factory) or when the source of the damage cannot be identified. That is why public responses are still needed.

blocks.text: Public responses to externalities
Pigouvian tax

text.text: is a tax levied on each unit of an externality generator's output in an amount equal to the marginal damage at the efficient level of output. The tax makes the polluter pay the cost it imposes on others, so its private cost becomes equal to the social cost and it reduces output to the efficient level.

blocks.text: Example: if each tonne of steel causes €20 of damage at the efficient output, the tax is €20 per tonne.
Subsidies

text.text: work the other way round. (Not in course slides: the government can pay a polluter for each unit by which it reduces pollution, or subsidise activities with positive externalities, such as vaccination or research.)

blocks.text: Emissions fee

text.text: is a tax levied on each unit of pollution. The difference from a Pigouvian tax: the Pigouvian tax is on each unit of OUTPUT; the emissions fee is on each unit of POLLUTION. (Not in course slides: taxing pollution directly lets a firm keep producing while cutting emissions, e.g. by installing a cleaner technology.)

blocks.text: Cap-and-trade

text.text: is a policy of granting permits to pollute, with the number of permits set at the desired pollution level, and allowing polluters to trade the permits. The "cap" fixes total pollution; the "trade" lets firms that can cut pollution cheaply sell their spare permits to firms for which cutting is expensive. Total pollution stays at the cap, and it is reduced where reduction is cheapest. (Example, not in course slides: the EU Emissions Trading System for CO₂.)

blocks.text: Incentive-based vs. command-and-control regulation

rows: Policies that provide polluters with financial incentives to reduce pollution
Policies that require a given amount of pollution reduction with limited or no flexibility with respect to how it may be achieved
Examples: Pigouvian tax, emissions fee, cap-and-trade
Examples: a rule that every plant must install a specific filter, or cut emissions by 30%
Firm chooses how much and how to reduce
Government dictates how much (and often how)

blocks.text: Hot spots

text.text: are localized concentrations of emissions. They are a risk of incentive-based systems: if one factory buys many permits, total pollution is at the cap, but the area around that factory gets heavily polluted.

blocks.text: Learn the exact pairs: Pigouvian tax = per unit of OUTPUT, equal to marginal damage at the efficient output; emissions fee = per unit of POLLUTION; cap-and-trade = permits set at the desired level and tradable; command-and-control = little or no flexibility.

blocks.text: Social security is the public pension and insurance system that pays benefits to retired workers, disabled workers and the dependents and survivors of covered workers. The slides follow the US system described in Rosen, and they show charts of social security expenditures in the US (1939–2011, source: Social Security Trustees 2012) and in the EU, both growing over time.
Why have social security?
1. Consumption smoothing and the annuity market

Social security provides insurance against the possibility of living longer than expected and so using up too early all the assets saved for retirement. It also provides benefits for disabled workers and for the dependents and survivors of disabled and retired workers.

items.text: – an insurance plan that charges a premium and then pays a sum of money at some regular interval for as long as the policyholder lives. The larger the premium, the larger the annual payments received in the future, other things being the same.
– reducing consumption in high-earning years in order to increase consumption in low-earning years. Example: saving part of your salary while working so you can keep spending in retirement.

blocks.text: 2. Adverse selection and the annuity market

text.text: Why can't private annuities do the job alone? Because of

: a situation in which one party to an economic transaction has better information about the good or service traded than the other party. A buyer of an annuity knows more about their own health and expected life span than the insurer, and the longer the buyer lives, the less money the seller makes. This causes a failure in the annuity market.

– the phenomenon under which the uninformed side of a deal gets exactly the wrong people trading with it. People who expect to live long buy annuities most eagerly; insurers raise prices to cover them; people with average life expectancy then find annuities too expensive and drop out. A compulsory public system covering everyone avoids this.

blocks.text: 3. Other justifications

items.text: – people may not save enough for old age, so the state forces them to.

– occurs when the existence of insurance increases the likelihood of the adverse outcome. Example: if people know the state will support them in old age anyway, they may save less (not in course slides: this argues for a compulsory system rather than relying on welfare).
Economize on decision-making and administrative costs
– one big public system can be cheaper than millions of individual decisions and private plans with high administrative costs.
– the benefit formula gives low earners relatively more.
Improve the economic status of the aged

blocks.text: Effects of social security on saving and behaviour

text.text: – an individual's consumption and saving decisions in a given year are based on a plan that considers lifetime circumstances. People save while working and spend savings in retirement. Social security changes this plan through three effects:

rows: Private saving is crowded out because social security already promises retirement income
If social security makes people retire earlier, they save more to finance a longer retirement
People may save more to leave a larger bequest to their children (e.g. to offset the taxes children pay for parents' benefits)

blocks.text: Because the effects go in opposite directions, theory alone cannot say whether social security lowers total saving; it is an empirical question (Rosen; not in course slides).
Long-term stresses on social security

items.text: – the ratio of social security beneficiaries to covered workers. As the population ages, there are more retirees per worker, which strains a pay-as-you-go system.
– the ratio of average social security benefits to average covered wages: how much of a typical wage the pension replaces.

learn.title: T5 Taxation and Income Distribution (Rosen, ch. 14)

blocks.text: This topic asks one question: who really pays a tax? The answer is often not the person who hands the money to the tax office.
Tax incidence: the basics

text.text: A firm, a building or a machine cannot carry a burden; in the end the burden falls on people: owners, workers or customers. To see which people, economists look at two ways of describing income distribution:

items.text: – the way income is distributed among people when they are classified according to the inputs they supply to the production process (workers, owners of capital, landowners).
– the way total income is distributed across income classes (low, middle, high income).

text.text: Both sources and uses of income should be considered.

A tax can hurt someone on the sources side (their wage or return falls) and on the uses side (the prices of the goods they buy rise). Example: a tax on bread lowers bakers' income (sources) and raises the price that poor households spend much of their income on (uses).

blocks.text: Statutory vs. economic incidence

rows: Who is legally responsible for the tax
The change in the distribution of private real income induced by a tax (who really ends up worse off)
The difference between statutory and economic incidence

blocks.text: Example: the law makes petrol stations pay an excise tax (statutory incidence). If stations raise pump prices, part of the burden is shifted to drivers (economic incidence).
What incidence depends on

items.text: – incidence differs in a competitive market, under monopoly or under oligopoly.
– what the government does with the money matters, because spending also changes incomes.

blocks.text: Three ways to handle the disposition of revenues:

items.text: – the combined effects of levying taxes and of the government spending financed by those taxes.
– the effect when one tax is replaced with another, holding the government budget constant. The usual reference tax is a
: a tax whose value is independent of the individual's behaviour (e.g. a fixed €500 per person, whatever they do).
– the effect of a tax when there is no change in either other taxes or government expenditure.

blocks.text: Measuring how progressive a tax is

items.text: – the ratio of taxes paid to income.
– the proportion of the last dollar of income taxed by the government.

rows: Stays constant regardless of income level
header: What happens to the AVERAGE tax rate as income rises

blocks.text: Progressivity is defined by the AVERAGE tax rate, not the marginal one. A flat-rate tax with a tax-free allowance has a constant marginal rate but a rising average rate, so it is progressive.
blocks.title: Common trap

blocks.text: Partial equilibrium models

text.text: study only one market and ignore possible spillover effects on other markets. In such a model the economic incidence of a tax depends on:

items.text: – (Rosen; not in course slides) the side of the market that reacts less to price (is more inelastic) bears more of the tax. Cigarette smokers react little to price, so they bear most of a cigarette tax.
– the extent to which a tax rate is made prominent to a taxpayer. A tax shown on the price tag is more salient than one added at the till, and people react more to salient taxes.

text.text: – the tax-induced difference between the price paid by consumers and the price received by producers. Example: before a €1 per unit tax the price is €5. After the tax consumers pay €5.70 and producers keep €4.70. The wedge is €1; consumers bear €0.70 and producers €0.30.

blocks.text: Ad valorem taxes

text.text: is computed as a percentage of the purchase value. The typical example is
, e.g. 25% in Croatia (standard rate; not in course slides). The alternative is a unit tax, a fixed amount per unit (Rosen; not in course slides).

blocks.text: Taxes on factors
Here statutory and economic incidence are compared for taxes on inputs:

items.text: – a tax on labour that finances social security (link to T4). (Rosen; not in course slides: the law splits it between employer and employee, but the economic incidence does not depend on that split. Because labour supply is fairly inelastic, workers bear most of it, also the "employer's" share, through lower wages.)
Tax on capital in a global economy
– (Rosen; not in course slides) capital can move to other countries, so it avoids much of a national tax; the burden shifts to factors that cannot move, such as workers and land.

blocks.text: Commodity taxation without competition

text.text: despite its market power, a monopolist is generally made worse off by a tax. After a tax:

items: The price paid by consumers goes up.
The price received by the monopolist goes down.

text.text: a tax can result in higher or lower profits; the outcome depends on how the few firms react to each other.

blocks.text: Profits taxes

text.text: Profits taxes are important for firms and companies.

is the return to the owners of a firm above the opportunity costs of all the factors used in production; it is also called supranormal or excess profit. (Rosen; not in course slides: a tax on economic profit cannot be shifted to customers or workers; the owners bear it.)

– a stream of tax liabilities becomes incorporated into the price of an asset. Example: if a new tax on a piece of land costs €1,000 every year, buyers will pay less for that land. The present value of all future taxes is subtracted from the price, so the owner at the moment the tax is announced bears the whole burden.

blocks.text: General equilibrium models

text.text: show how various markets are interrelated: a tax in one market changes prices and incomes in others. They often use a two-sector, two-factor model (e.g. two goods, labour and capital).
pioneered the application of general equilibrium models to tax incidence.

blocks.text: T5 asked who pays a tax. T6 asks a different question: how much does a tax cost the economy beyond the money it raises?
Excess burden

text.text: : a cost beyond the tax revenue collected. It is a loss of welfare above and beyond the taxes collected, also called the

items.text: tax-induced distortions in behaviour. People change what they buy or how much they work because of the tax, not because their real preferences or costs changed.
with either indifference curves or compensated demand curves.

blocks.text: Example (illustrative): a high tax is put on chocolate. Ana, who loves chocolate, switches to biscuits she likes less. She pays no chocolate tax, so the government collects nothing from her, but she is still worse off. That loss, with no revenue in return, is pure excess burden.
Lump-sum taxes: the benchmark

text.text: is a tax whose value is independent of the individual's behaviour (e.g. every adult pays €500, whatever they earn or buy). Because nothing you do changes the tax, it does not distort behaviour and creates no excess burden.

items: Lump-sum taxes are unattractive as policy tools. (Rosen; not in course slides: a poor person and a rich person pay the same amount, which most people see as unfair.)
Nevertheless, they are an important standard against which the excess burdens of other taxes are compared.

blocks.text: (The formula is from Rosen, not the slides: η = compensated elasticity of demand, P and Q = price and quantity before the tax, t = ad valorem tax rate.)

items: Doubling the tax rate makes the excess burden four times larger (2² = 4). Many small taxes on different goods are therefore usually less costly than one big tax.
The more elastic the compensated demand, the bigger the excess burden: people can easily switch away, so the tax distorts a lot. Taxing goods with inelastic demand creates less excess burden.

blocks.text: Excess-burden calculations usually assume no other distortions. If other distortions exist (e.g. another tax or a monopoly), the incremental excess burden of a new tax depends on its effects in other markets too.
blocks.title: When other distortions exist

blocks.text: Subsidies and taxes on inputs also create excess burden

text.text: create excess burdens because they encourage people to consume goods valued less than the marginal social cost of production. Example: if a good costs €10 to produce but a subsidy lets people buy it for €6, people buy units they value at only €7: each such unit wastes €3 of resources.

creates an excess burden. When the same input (e.g. capital) is taxed in one activity and not in another, it is used "too little" in the taxed activities and "too much" in the untaxed activities. Example (illustrative): if capital in the corporate sector is taxed more heavily than in housing, too much capital flows into housing.

blocks.text: Theory of the second best

text.text: – in the presence of existing distortions, policies that in isolation would increase efficiency can decrease it, and vice versa.

blocks.text: Example (illustrative): if coffee is already heavily taxed, putting a tax on tea (a substitute) could actually improve efficiency, because it reduces the distortion between coffee and tea. In a world without the coffee tax, the same tea tax would only add excess burden.

Lump-sum tax appears in both T5 (as the reference tax for differential incidence) and T6 (as the tax with no excess burden). Learn the T6 rule word by word: excess burden is proportional to the compensated elasticity of demand and to the square of the tax rate. T7 (Efficient and Equitable Taxation) builds on this.
